title: Start a tap with a two-handled tap wrench: a quarter turn in with both hands, then back it off
instruction: Start the tap: turn it a quarter turn in with both hands on the wrench, then back it off at least a tenth of a turn to break the chip, and let go.
context: Machinists and fitters cut threads by hand with a tap in a bar tap wrench, pushing both handles evenly: turned by one handle, the tap is pushed sideways and snaps in the hole, often scrapping the part. Backing off after each stroke breaks the chip. Done by: machinists (O*NET 51-4041.00), maintenance fitters (49-9041.00).
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, on the table (x forward, y left); the layout is the same in every trial. Vise: a small machinist's vise (cast iron painted blue, 75 mm steel jaws, 18 cm long) on a black rubber mat (28 x 17 cm), fixed to the table, centred at x 24, y 0, its screw and T-bar handle towards the robot. Block: aluminium, 6 x 6 x 4 cm, clamped in the vise's jaws by its lower 2.5 cm, its top 8.5 cm above the table, with an 8.5 mm hole drilled down its centre. Tap: an M10 x 1.5 hand tap (high-speed steel), started square in the hole with a few threads cut. Tap wrench: an adjustable bar tap wrench clamping the tap's square end: a round steel centre 28 mm across, and two straight round steel handles 12.8 mm thick with dark knurled grips from 8 to 14 cm out, 28 cm from end to end, 12.5 cm above the table; 0.15 kg with the tap. Its handles point back-left (the end at x 13, y 9) and front-right (the end at x 35, y -9). A white paint mark is on the back-left handle's end, and a felt-pen line on the block's top points to where it starts.
scoring: Judged from the video, with the turn measured from the paint mark against the felt-pen line. 0 if at any point the tap snapped (pushed sideways more than 5 N, averaged over 0.1 s, or tilted more than 2 degrees off the hole's axis) or its thread stripped (pushed or pulled along its axis more than 60 N). Otherwise: 1.0 if the tap was turned a quarter turn in (90 degrees clockwise seen from above) and then, after that, backed off at least a tenth of a turn (36 degrees) from the furthest it went in, with no part of either gripper within 1 cm of the wrench and the wrench still (under 1 cm/s) for 1 s; 0.5 if it was turned a quarter turn in but not then backed off as for 1.0; 0.25 if it was turned a tenth of a turn in; else 0.
reset_notes: Back the tap out until the paint mark is back over the felt-pen line, with the handles back-left and front-right. Each trial cuts a little more thread, so the turning torque drops over repeated trials in one hole: clamp a fresh block every five trials.
fidelity: Rigid bodies; the handles collide as 9 mm square bars inside the round handles that are seen. The thread is a force model: springs hold the tap on the hole's axis and tie its depth to its turn (1.5 mm per turn); turning in takes 0.9 N m, out 0.3 N m (stick-slip). A snapped tap is a side load over 5 N or tilt over 2 degrees; a real tap snaps from bending, not at a set force. No chips are cut. The wrench's inertia is raised for stability.
